---
title: "BECS Interfaces and Data Integrity"
order: 53
---

## Six boundaries, one last review

VAL-1203 — Lakeshore's upgrade of BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) to the vendor's
next major release, Release B — has been live for a full quarter now. The periodic review closed
last module with a real finding: VIA-0842's twelve tests were never shown adequate, because nobody
ever wrote the regression analysis that should have scoped them. Remediation is already running —
a regression-analysis requirement for every future OS-patch VIA (validation impact assessment,
the term this course has used since module 1 for the document that decides whether a change needs
new testing), plus targeted supplemental testing aimed at the three places that analysis would
have reached: instrument interfaces, the hospital interface, and label-print timing under peak
load.

That supplemental testing is this module's subject. Your Quality Validation Lead brings you one
more document before calling VAL-1203 fully closed out: a short section of the validation report,
written specifically about BECS's interfaces — every boundary where data crosses from one system
into BECS, or out of BECS into something else. Six of them, as Release B's cutover actually
exercised them:

| # | Boundary | What crosses it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Instruments and the testing lab's LIS (laboratory information system) | Test results and quarantine status, inbound |
| 2 | BECS to label printers | Label data, outbound |
| 3 | ICCBBA (International Council for Commonality in Blood Banking Automation) reference tables into BECS | Product-code reference data, inbound |
| 4 | BECS to Riverside General Hospital | Electronic shipment data, outbound |
| 5 | Central BECS to Brookfield and Fairview | Donor, unit, and quarantine data, both directions |
| 6 | Legacy data conversion (Release A to Release B) | Donor and deferral history, one-time |

Your job today isn't to re-run any of this testing. It's to read what's in front of you,
boundary by boundary, and ask the same question six times: does this evidence actually prove a
record lands complete, correct, on time, and on the right donor or unit — or does it just prove
the connection works? Two of these six boundaries carry extra weight. One of them is where
VIA-0842 — the deviation this whole course was built around — left an open note nobody ever
assigned to anyone: "BECS-to-hospital interface regression testing to follow." Another is a test
type VIA-0842's twelve cases never included at all. By the end of this module both are closed, for
real, not just reported closed.

## Why this matters, and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module exists to catch: every individual interface can "work" — connect,
send, receive, log no errors — while the thing that actually matters, a specific record reaching
a specific destination intact and on time, still fails. A connection test and a data-integrity
test are not the same test, and a package that only ran the first one has proven far less than it
looks like it has.

You already own the ITSM (IT service management) vocabulary for this. **Integration and
middleware monitoring** — watching the pipes between systems, not just the systems themselves —
is a practice you run constantly, and every mature integration has a **dead-letter queue**: the
place a message lands when it can't be processed, so it doesn't just vanish. FDA's BECS guidance
has its own name for exactly that idea, written years before anyone called it a dead-letter queue:
an **interface error file**. Same concept, same reason it exists — something came across the wire
the receiving system couldn't handle, and it has to land somewhere visible instead of silently
disappearing. **Reconciliation jobs** are the other half: periodically checking that what left one
system actually arrived, intact, at the other.

Here's where the regulated world asks more of you than an ordinary ITSM practice does. In
ordinary IT operations, a message that lands in a dead-letter queue is a data-quality issue or an
integration bug — annoying, triaged, fixed on a normal backlog. On BECS, a message that lands on
the *wrong* record isn't an outage to fix and move on from. It's a potential product-safety event:
a unit released under the wrong donor's eligibility status, a quarantine that didn't propagate
before a unit shipped. Same technical failure, very different seriousness, because of what's on
the other end of the wire.

## The rule in plain English

**First, and worth saying plainly: Lakeshore is a blood center, not a hospital, and its interface
inventory looks nothing like the one FDA's own guidance uses as its example.** FDA's BECS
guidance talks about validating interfaces to a **HIS** (Hospital Information System — things
like ADT, admissions/discharges/transfers) and an **LIS** (Laboratory Information System — things
like OE/RR, order entry/results return). That language makes sense for the guidance's own
illustrative setting: a hospital transfusion service running BECS, sitting inside the same
building as the HIS that admits patients and the LIS that orders their labs. Lakeshore doesn't
have an HIS. Lakeshore doesn't admit patients. A learner who copied that sentence onto Lakeshore's
own validation plan — "validate our HIS/ADT interface" — would be describing an interface
Lakeshore doesn't have, while missing every interface it actually does. The six boundaries in the
table above are Lakeshore's real inventory, and they earn that status the same way the guidance's
own examples do: each one is a place where a record crosses from one system's control into
another's, and has to arrive intact on the far side.

**Second: the standard every one of these six boundaries has to meet is the same four-part test,
every time.** Does the record that crosses this boundary land *complete* (nothing missing), is it
*correct* (nothing corrupted or mistranslated on the way), does it arrive *on time* (not sitting
in a queue past the point it needed to act), and does it land on the *right donor or unit* (not
silently attached to the wrong record)? A connectivity test answers none of those four questions
by itself. An interface validated well enough to trust has to answer all four.

**Third: quarantine-status propagation latency is its own question, and a thorough interface
validation has to ask it everywhere, not just test each interface in isolation.** When a unit's
status changes — a late-arriving positive test result triggers a quarantine — how fast does that
new status actually reach every system that needs to know: the label printer, the hospital-
shipment interface, each satellite site's BECS client? If the answer is "eventually," that's a real
gap even if every interface, tested on its own, passes cleanly. A unit can be correctly flagged
inside BECS and still ship, print, or release somewhere downstream before the flag catches up.

**Fourth: who validates what, across an organizational boundary, follows control — it isn't a
rule anyone writes down.** Lakeshore validates what it sends and what it receives, at its own side
of each boundary. Riverside General Hospital — the fictional 340-bed hospital Lakeshore ships
components to, your established consignee — validates its own systems, under its own obligations.
Nobody assigns that split by regulation; it's the practical, sensible allocation: you validate what
you control, and stop at the point you no longer control it. Where the two sides' expectations of
each other actually get written down is the supplier/customer relationship itself — the kind of
territory AABB's (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) **QSE 4, Suppliers and
Customers** theme, named earlier in this course, covers. No standard number here, just the theme.

**Fifth, briefly: one more acronym belongs in this lesson, named and pointed forward, not
developed.** Complete, correct, on time, right donor or unit is this module's own vocabulary for
data integrity at an interface. The data-integrity field has a more formal name for the fuller set
of properties a record has to hold: **ALCOA+** — attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original,
accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring, and available. `data-integrity-and-records`, a
future course, is where that framework gets its real depth, including audit-trail review in
practice. Here, know the name exists.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guidance III.G (interfaces) | "Section three, part G" | Recommends validating all interfaces, including HIS/ADT, LIS/OE-RR, and instrument interfaces, and continuing to monitor interface error files after implementation. | The guidance's own hospital-shaped list — and the reason Lakeshore has to translate it, not copy it. |
| Guidance III.G (legacy conversion) | "Section three, part G" | Recommends validating the data conversion from a legacy system to a new one, to avoid duplicate donor records and deferral codes. | VAL-1203's own Release A to Release B cutover, boundary six. |
| Guidance III.J | "Section three, part J" | Recommends determining what functions or files an integrated LIS/HIS and BECS share, by discussing it with the BECS manufacturer, before assuming a change to one doesn't touch the other. | Lakeshore's version: the testing-lab's LIS, and the vendor's own suite of modules. |
| 21 CFR 211.68(b) | "Two-eleven point sixty-eight, paragraph b" | Input to and output from a computer system must be checked for accuracy, with the degree and frequency of that verification scaled to the system's complexity and reliability. | The regulatory floor under every one of these six boundaries — each is an input/output point this paragraph already governs. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(h) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph h" | Device checks: determining, as appropriate, the validity of the source of data input or an operational instruction. | Does BECS actually verify a result came from the instrument it claims to, rather than accepting whatever arrives on that channel? |
| 21 CFR 606.165(b)/(c) | "Six-oh-six point one sixty-five, paragraphs b and c" | Distribution records must identify the consignee, delivery date and quantity, lot number, and expiration or collection date; receipt records mirror that same information. | Applied here to the *electronic* shipment-data interface to Riverside, not the paper record this course already covered. |

## The actual text, boundary by boundary

**Boundary 1 — instruments and the testing-lab LIS.** This is where the in-house Category 5
translation script lives — the one this course has carried since module 1, still sitting on its own
unresolved question (is building it enough to make Lakeshore a "manufacturer"? still routed to
regulatory affairs, still not this module's to answer). The guidance's interface recommendation,
quoted verbatim from `sources/fda-guidance/becs-validation-users-facility-2013.md`, section III.G:

> We recommend that you qualify equipment, validate all interfaces, including those to a Hospital
> Information System (HIS) (e.g., admissions, discharges and transfers (ADT)); a Laboratory
> Information System (LIS) (e.g., order entry/results return (OE/RR)); and all instrument
> interfaces, as applicable. Monitoring of interface error files should continue subsequent to
> implementation as unforeseen transaction types or data elements may cause disastrous results
> (for instance, orders not being received, results posting to the incorrect donor/patient record,
> etc.).

Read "LIS (OE/RR)" for what it actually maps to here: not a hospital's lab ordering results back
to a clinician, but Lakeshore's own testing lab feeding infectious-disease marker results and
quarantine status into BECS, through the in-house script. "Instrument interfaces" is the same
boundary from one step further back — the analyzers themselves. And "results posting to the
incorrect donor/patient record" is the guidance's own example of exactly the failure this boundary
has to prove it doesn't make.

**Boundary 2 — BECS to label printers.** This is the same boundary VIA-0842's own step 7 tested —
label-print job timing at the primary print station — except this course now has the vocabulary
to see it correctly: not a one-off test case, an *interface*, with its own complete/correct/on-time
standard. A label that prints the wrong product code, or prints before a late status change lands,
is this boundary's version of the same failure.

**Boundary 3 — ICCBBA reference tables into BECS.** ICCBBA maintains the product-code reference
tables BECS uses to print and read labels correctly. This is the inbound boundary behind DEV-1147, already established
in this curriculum: an ICCBBA table push that reached BECS at 01:58 a.m. on a Wednesday, with
roughly forty units printed one revision behind before the Processing Supervisor caught it — a
deviation this module doesn't re-litigate, and leaves exactly as written. What matters here is the
shape: an inbound interface carrying reference data, not test results, no less capable of causing a
labeling failure than one carrying donor-specific information.

**Boundary 4 — BECS to Riverside General Hospital.** Riverside is Lakeshore's established
consignee, already governed at the paper-and-process level by 21 CFR 606.165, distribution and
receipt records. Here, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.165.md`, is the same text applied to
the *electronic* version of that same obligation:

> (b) Distribution records shall contain information to readily facilitate the identification of
> the name and address of the consignee, the date and quantity delivered, the lot number of the
> unit(s), the date of expiration or the date of collection, whichever is applicable, or for
> crossmatched blood and blood components, the name of the recipient.
>
> (c) Receipt records shall contain the name and address of the collecting facility, date
> received, donor or lot number assigned by the collecting facility and the date of expiration or
> the date of collection, whichever is applicable.

Nothing in that text cares whether the record travels on a packing slip or an electronic
shipment-data feed. The same fields — consignee, date, quantity, lot number, expiration or
collection date — have to be provably accurate either way. An electronic interface just moves
where the proof has to come from: a test showing the feed reproduces those fields correctly, not a
paper form filed afterward.

**Boundary 5 — central BECS to Brookfield and Fairview.** Module 3 already asked whether each
satellite site has its own validation plan — a question about *scope*. This is a different
question, about the *data* moving across that same link: when a unit's status changes centrally,
how fast does Brookfield's or Fairview's own BECS client see it? A satellite site running on
stale data isn't a scope gap. It's this boundary's version of the complete/correct/on-time
standard failing in a specific, local way.

**Boundary 6 — legacy data conversion.** VAL-1203's own Release A to Release B cutover carried old
data into the new system — exactly the situation the guidance's last validation-activities bullet
addresses, quoted verbatim:

> Although not a function of your system, we recommend that you validate the data conversion from
> your legacy system to your new system to avoid problems such as duplicate donor records and
> deferral codes.

Read "duplicate donor records" and "deferral codes" as the two sharpest ways a conversion can fail
silently: the same donor ending up as two records nobody links, or a deferral that existed in the
old system not carrying forward into the new one. Either failure is invisible until someone goes
looking for it specifically — which is exactly why the guidance calls it out as its own validation
activity, separate from testing the system's ordinary functions.

**One more piece, cutting across all six: is BECS an integrated package, or a stand-alone
system?** The guidance's own framing, quoted in full from section III.J:

> If your system or BECS is part of an integrated package on a Laboratory Information System (LIS)
> or Hospital Information System (HIS) rather than a stand-alone system, you should also consider
> how changes made to functionality shared by the LIS or HIS and BECS (such as ADT, orders, etc.)
> might affect your system or BECS. You should determine what functions or files your LIS or HIS
> and your BECS share by discussing this with your BECS manufacturer.

Translate that honestly for Lakeshore: the question was never "is BECS integrated with a
hospital's LIS or HIS," because Lakeshore has neither. The real question is "is BECS integrated
with the testing lab's own LIS, or with the vendor's own suite of modules, closely enough that a
change to one could silently move the other?" The principle survives the translation untouched:
know what's shared, and know, in writing, whose job it is to validate the shared piece when either
side changes it.

**Underneath every one of these, the regulatory floor is the same paragraph, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/211.68.md`:**

> (b) Appropriate controls shall be exercised over computer or related systems to assure that
> changes in master production and control records or other records are instituted only by
> authorized personnel. Input to and output from the computer or related system of formulas or
> other records or data shall be checked for accuracy. The degree and frequency of input/output
> verification shall be based on the complexity and reliability of the computer or related system.

Read that against the six-boundary table: every one of them is an input/output point this
paragraph already reaches. 211.68(a), this course's first citation, is the floor behind validating
a system at all. (b) is the floor behind validating what crosses its edges — and "degree and
frequency... based on the complexity and reliability" is 211.68's own permission to scale scrutiny:
a reference-table feed and a hospital-shipment feed don't need identical rigor, but neither gets a
free pass.

**And one control worth a brief requote, already quoted in full back in module 5, which
deliberately deferred its depth to here:** 21 CFR 11.10(h), from `sources/cfr/11.10.md`:

> (h) Use of device (e.g., terminal) checks to determine, as appropriate, the validity of the
> source of data input or operational instruction.

Apply it concretely, at every one of the six boundaries: does BECS actually verify that a result
claiming to come from a specific instrument, a specific satellite site, or a specific reference-
table push really did come from there — or does it just accept whatever arrives on that channel,
trusting the label the message carries about its own origin? A system that can be fed a convincing
but false message, and can't tell the difference, hasn't satisfied (h), no matter how fast or
reliable the channel otherwise is.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reading this section of VAL-1203's file wouldn't stop at "an
interface exists and a connection test passed." They'd ask, boundary by boundary, for a test that
actually tried to break the four-part standard — a malformed or duplicate result message sent on
purpose, not just a clean one; a reconciliation record showing what left one system matches what
arrived at the other; a dated check of how long a quarantine status took to reach every downstream
system, not an assumption that it's instant. They'd also ask where the interface error file —
Lakeshore's dead-letter queue, in the guidance's own words — actually is, who reviews it, and how
often, since the guidance's own sentence says monitoring "should continue subsequent to
implementation," not stop once go-live testing passed.

A bad answer to "how do you know a result always lands on the right donor" sounds like "the
interface has never thrown an error." A good answer points to a test that sent a message with the
wrong identifier on purpose, and a record showing BECS caught it.

## Common traps

**"The interface connects and logs no errors, so it's validated."** This is the connectivity-test
trap, and it's the direct cousin of module 6's "it installed without errors, so it's validated."
A clean connection proves the pipe works. It proves nothing about whether a specific message
landed complete, correct, on time, and on the right donor or unit — the four things 211.68(b) and
the guidance's interface recommendation actually require evidence of. Only a test that tried a
malformed, duplicate, or out-of-order message, and checked where it landed, can answer that.

**"Riverside's LIS is part of our validation, since our shipment data feeds it."** No. Riverside
General Hospital's own information systems are Riverside's to validate, under its own obligations
— Lakeshore validates what it sends and receives, at its own side of the boundary. Responsibility
follows control, not the fact that data crosses an organizational line. The two parties'
agreement, the kind of territory AABB's Suppliers and Customers theme covers, is where each side's
expectations of the other actually get written down — not a shared validation obligation that
doesn't exist.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask for a test that tried to break each interface, not one that confirmed it connects.** A
  malformed message, a duplicate, an out-of-order arrival, a wrong identifier on purpose — if none
  of those were ever tried, the interface has been connected, not validated.
- **Ask who reviews the interface error file, and how often.** The guidance's own words are
  "should continue subsequent to implementation" — a dead-letter queue nobody has opened since
  go-live is a gap you'll find before an inspector does, if you ask now.
- **Ask the quarantine-propagation-latency question at every boundary, not just one.** A status
  change that reaches BECS instantly but takes minutes to reach a satellite client or a label
  printer is a real patient-safety gap, even though every interface, tested alone, passed.
- **Keep Lakeshore's validation scoped to Lakeshore's side of every external boundary**, and treat
  a message landing on the wrong record as a product-safety event from the first minute, not an
  integration bug on a normal backlog — the one habit an ordinary ITSM incident process won't
  supply on its own.

## Closing VIA-0842's last two open items

This course opened with VIA-0842's twelve tests and a question nobody could answer yet. Module 6
answered the methodological half: the number twelve was never the defect, the missing regression
analysis was. That finding prescribed targeted supplemental testing, not a full revalidation —
aimed specifically at instrument interfaces, the hospital interface, and label timing under peak
load. Here is that testing, finally carried out, closing the two pieces of VIA-0842's own record
that were left open on purpose.

**First: VIA-0842's twelve tests never included an instrument-interface test at all.** That gap
sat unaddressed through this entire course, because closing it required exactly the method this
course exists to teach: a documented regression analysis, not a guess, saying where to look. That
analysis — module 6's own positive-contrast patch VIA already modeled it correctly — named
instrument interfaces as one of the three places an OS-level memory-handling change plausibly
reaches. The supplemental test that followed did what VIA-0842 never did: sent a result message
with a deliberately malformed field, a duplicate donation identifier, and an out-of-order arrival
through the instrument-to-BECS path, and checked not just that BECS logged an error, but that
nothing landed silently on the wrong donor's record. It passed — but passing only means something
because the test could have failed, the same lesson module 2 built this course's whole approach to
test-case anatomy around.

**Second: VIA-0842's own unresolved note — "BECS-to-hospital interface regression testing to
follow" — never had an owner or a date.** It has one now. The Quality Validation Lead took it as
the owner, with a dated target inside this same supplemental-testing cycle, and the test that
closed it is the Riverside shipment-data interface specifically: a test shipment record, sent
through the electronic interface exactly as a real one would be, checked field by field against
606.165(b)'s and (c)'s own list — consignee name and address, date and quantity, lot number,
expiration or collection date — to confirm the electronic version carries every one of those
fields correctly, not just that the file transmitted.

**Neither of these rewrites VIA-0842's own record.** Its twelve tests, its step 7, its Wednesday
10:15 p.m. deployment, its unassigned open note — all of that stays exactly as this course has
always described it. What's different is that the work that note promised finally happened, with
an owner, a date, and evidence behind it, as part of the supplemental testing module 6 prescribed.
That's the whole difference between a deviation record and the system it describes: the record is
closed history. The system kept being validated after it.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: A colleague says, "Riverside's LIS is part of our validation, since our shipment data feeds it." Accurate?

No. Riverside General Hospital's own information systems are Riverside's to validate, under its
own obligations — not Lakeshore's. Lakeshore validates what it sends and what it receives, at its
own side of the BECS-to-Riverside boundary: does the shipment-data feed accurately carry the
606.165(b)/(c) fields (consignee, date and quantity, lot number, expiration or collection date)
when it leaves Lakeshore's systems. What Riverside does with that data once it lands on its own
systems is Riverside's validation to perform. This is responsibility following control, not a rule
either party's regulation states outright — and the agreement between the two organizations, the
kind of territory AABB's Suppliers and Customers theme covers, is where each side's expectations of
the other actually get spelled out.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: VAL-1203's interface section shows every one of the six boundaries connected successfully during cutover, with zero connection errors logged. Does that mean the interfaces are validated?

No, and this is the connectivity-test trap this module is built to catch. A clean connection with
zero logged errors proves the pipe works. It says nothing about whether a specific record crossing
that boundary lands complete, correct, on time, and on the right donor or unit — the actual
standard 211.68(b) and the guidance's interface recommendation require evidence of. Only a test
that deliberately tried a malformed message, a duplicate, an out-of-order arrival, or a wrong
identifier, and confirmed where it landed, proves that. "It connects without errors" is this
module's version of module 6's "it installed without errors" — implementation evidence, not
validation evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: FDA's BECS guidance names HIS/ADT and LIS/OE/RR interfaces as examples to validate. Should Lakeshore's validation plan list those two interfaces by name?

No — and getting this wrong is the sharpest trap this module names. HIS (Hospital Information
System, things like admissions/discharges/transfers) and LIS (Laboratory Information System,
order entry/results return) are the guidance's own illustrative examples, written for a hospital
transfusion service running BECS. Lakeshore is a blood center, not a hospital: it has no HIS, and
its own testing lab's LIS feeds results into BECS through the in-house translation script, not
through an ADT-style hospital feed. A validation plan that copies "HIS/ADT interface" onto
Lakeshore's own documentation would be describing an interface Lakeshore doesn't have, while
leaving its actual six boundaries — instruments and the testing lab, label printers, ICCBBA
tables, the hospital shipment-data feed, the satellite sites, and legacy-data conversion —
unaddressed. The guidance's principle (validate every interface, monitor error files afterward)
transfers. Its specific example list does not.
:::

## Where this goes next

This course opened by naming VIA-0842's twelve tests and a question nobody could answer. It built
the answer in pieces: GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice) and the V-model gave you the
vocabulary to sort software and size a risk assessment instead of trusting a category label. IQ,
OQ, PQ, and the traceability matrix taught you to read executed evidence and tell a test that could
fail from one that never really tried. BECS as a regulated device, and the vendor's own QMSR
(Quality Management System Regulation) and ISO 13485 world, placed Lakeshore correctly under blood
CGMP (current good manufacturing practice) while the device-grade rules bind the vendor instead.
Part 11 named the specific electronic-records controls a validation has to prove the system
enforces, not just document. Staying validated gave VIA-0842 its real verdict: not a number that
was wrong, but an analysis that was never written. And this module closed what that verdict left
open — the instrument-interface test VIA-0842 never ran, and the hospital-interface regression
testing its own record promised and never assigned.

Both of VIA-0842's open interface items are closed now, for real, with evidence behind them. That's
the course's finish line, reached in full.

Two things stay open on purpose, and they were always meant to. The in-house script's "is
Lakeshore a manufacturer" question is still sitting with regulatory affairs — not this course's
call, and not resolved here either. And everything this module touched only lightly — ALCOA+ in
full depth, audit-trail review in practice, the predicate-rule doctrine Part 11 rests on, unique
donor identification across systems — belongs to `data-integrity-and-records`, a future course,
where it finally gets the treatment this one only pointed toward.

You came into this course able to route a validation question to someone else. You leave it able
to read the package yourself, ask the question an inspector would ask, and know exactly what's
still missing. That's the finish line this course set out to reach.
